questions.q: According to this lesson, why do cost and latency need active monitoring even when an AI system is working exactly as designed?
options: Because cost and latency scale with traffic and token volume, so 'working as designed' at much higher traffic can still mean a tripled bill or a suddenly slow product
Because cost and latency never change once a system is deployed
Because only broken systems have variable cost or latency
Because monitoring cost and latency is only required for free-tier AI products
questions.explain: Unlike catching something going wrong, cost and latency are usually working as intended, but they scale with usage in ways that still need watching.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a single 'total cost this month' number is less useful than a dashboard broken out by model, time, and session?
options: A single total number is always more accurate than any breakdown
A single total doesn't make a spike traceable to a specific cause, while a breakdown by dimension does
Breaking out cost by dimension is impossible with real observability tools
Dashboards only need to show the current month, never historical trends
questions.explain: Breaking cost and latency out by model, country, and time is what lets a spike be traced to an actual cause instead of just noticing a number went up.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say per-session cost and latency metrics matter more than per-call metrics for a multi-step agent?
options: Per-call metrics are always identical to per-session metrics
Sessions are never used by multi-step AI agents
A multi-step agent session can involve many calls before returning an answer, so the session total is where the real expense actually shows up
Per-session metrics replace the need to track cost at all
questions.explain: Looking only at the last call in a session would hide the cumulative cost and time of all the calls that led up to it.

questions.q: How does caching reduce both cost and latency at the same time, according to this lesson?
options: Caching only reduces latency and has no effect on cost
Caching requires sending the request to a more expensive model
Caching deletes the original request so it can never be billed
A repeated or near-identical request is served from a stored response instead of triggering a new model call
questions.explain: Skipping the model call entirely on a cache hit avoids both the token cost and the wait time of a fresh call.

questions.q: What does knowing a provider's per-million-token pricing, as shown in this lesson, actually enable?
options: Routing simpler tasks to a cheaper model instead of defaulting every call to the most expensive option
Guaranteeing that latency will always be zero regardless of model choice
Eliminating the need to track cost once pricing is known
Making every model cost exactly the same regardless of provider
questions.explain: Since per-million-token prices can differ five to ten times across models, knowing that gap is the basis for intentionally routing cheaper tasks to cheaper models.
